Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure respecting the Canadian National Railways, to authorize the provision of moneys to meet expenditures made and indebtedness incurred during the calendar year, 1934, and to provide for the refunding of certain maturing financial obligations.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the bill which it is intended to found on this resolution is designed to take care of the full financial requirements of the Canadian National Railways for the calendar year 1934. It provides for the raising of funds for equipment principal payments, sinking funds, and miscellaneous maturing obligations amounting to $12,185,828; for' construction and betterments $4,202,007 and for the estimated net income deficits amounting to $48,840,298. These amounts, in particular as respects the contemplated deficits, are arrived at as a result
C.N.R.-Finance

of a report which has been received from the trustees of the railway system in conformity with the act. That makes the total sum required for the railway's operation under the headings I have mentioned $65,228,133.
The bill is in two parts. The first part has to do with what might be termed the ordinary financial requirements of the railway for the year. The second part makes provision for the refunding of two maturities for the calendar year, the first one falling due September 1, 1934, and amounting to $17,060,333.33, Canadian Northern four per cent guaranteed debenture stock and bonds; also Great Northern Railway of Canada four per cent first mortgage bonds falling due October 1, 1934, amounting to $3,510,250. It also provides for the refunding of a maturity falling due on February 15, 1935, Canadian Northern Railway Company 4jj per cent guaranteed bonds, amounting to $17,000,000. It was thought wise that we should secure at this time legislative authority to refund or otherwise take care of that maturity lest there might not be time to secure legislative authority having regard to the date at which the session might commence.

Hon. E. N. RHODES moved the second reading of Bill No. 55, to provide for the deduction from compensation in the public service.
He said, Mr. Speaker, there is nothing that I feel I can usefully add to what was said when this bill was introduced. I can certainly add nothing to what was said in previous years at very great length in connection with similar measures which it has been our duty to consider. This year we have been able to make a partial restoration in full of salaries. It would have been a much more pleasing duty on my part, and much more pleasing to the government and to the house as a whole, could we have gone the full distance. That we do not do so is due entirely to the limitation imposed upon us by our revenues. That is the sole reason, and I may say that we shall be only too delighted, when the time arrives and the treasury will permit us to do so, to restore in full the salaries which have been reduced during the past two or three years.

subtopic: SALARY DEDUCTION ACT-RESTORATION OF TEN PER CENT CUT TO EMPLOYEES RECEIVING $1,000 OR LESS
speechtext:
Before the motion carries for the second reading I wish to make a few observations. I do not intend to delay the house at any great length, but we are confronted with a situation which I think calls for consideration in view of the decision which you, Mr. Speaker, gave a few days ago with respect to another bill. I voted against Your Honour's interpretation of the rule with respect to amendments to the second reading of bills, but the majority of hon. members sustained that ruling. We are now on the second reading of Bill No. 55, and that means that we are concerned with its principle. The principle of the bill may be ascertained in the same manner as the principle of the marketing bill was sought to be ascertained when that measure was before the house. This bill is "An Act to Provide for the Deduction from Compensation in the Public Service." The short title' of the bill is:
This act may be cited as The Salary Deduction (Continuance) Act, 1934.
Section 3 of the bill reads:
Notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law, there shall, during the fiscal year ending the 31st day of March, 1935, be deducted from the compensation of every member of the public service of Canada 10 per centum of the amount thereof: Provided-[DOT]
Now I submit that the principle of this bill is not to be found in any rider to the bill; we are not concerned with the principle of the rider. We are not concerned with the principle of the provision but, I submit, with the principle of the bill itself, and that principle is double-barrelled in that it is for the continuance of the deduction from compensa-

tion in the public service. It is true that by the rider in the bill, an amendment to the law, some small minority will be affected in an infinitesimal way, and I suppose that in times of stress such as the present, with a government in power such as we have to-day, for these small mercies we ought to be grateful. But my attitude to these salary reductions is well known both in this house and elsewhere, and I for one cannot accept the principle of a continuance of the deduction from these salaries.
Now, the Minister of Finance, in introducing the bill, said that a certain range would be affected. I quote:
That range takes in a very large number of employees of the public service. As nearly as we can ascertain some eighteen thousand in number will be affected, including revenue postmasters, part time collectors of customs, lighthouse keepers, wharfingers, charwomen, seasonal or part time labourers, lockmen and bridgemen on the canals. Those in receipt of salaries above the sum of $1,000 will be subject to the same deduction as hitherto.
Therefore, right on the face of it, there is one class of the two classes of the service, those engaged in the service of the state, that will benefit, one small portion of a huge class. The government, at the time they decided upon this most unfortunate policy, were careful to make these deductions as heavy as possible upon both classes of the service-the public service at large and the civil service, so-called. This bill means something or it means nothing. If it means anything, it means something in the way of deduction. But after all, what does it mean in a practical way? I am sure that if the minister had been properly advised, or if he had followed his own sagacity and had gone carefully into the measure, he would not have brought down this picayune concession to those affected; because, with all deference to the hon. gentleman, for whom I have the highest regard, I am bound to say that the restoration of 10 per cent to those who will benefit is absolutely ridiculous. Let us see how far the generosity of the government, under the most difficult circumstances to which the minister has referred, will go, and to what extent the 18,000 employees referred to will benefit. Is this to be a smoke screen or a camouflage?
I take the report of the civil service committee for 1932 and I find in appendix J the total number of permanent and temporary employees in the civil service so-called of Ottawa, as of March, 1931, which is the last figure available, was 11,766 and the total

Civil Service-Salary Deduction
number outside Ottawa for the same date was 33,815, making the total number in Canada 45.581. Therefore there is in Ottawa about 30 per cent and outside Ottawa about 70 per cent of the classified service, so that when one speaks about the civil service one speaks not for the civil service of Ottawa alone but for 100 per cent of the civil service wherever in Canada those employees may 'be located.
When I look at appendix C of the same report, what do I find? The minister said that he was returning the salary deduction to all those who receive $1,000 or less. Included in that number let us see how many are in the classified service and how many in the non-classified service, and how they compare with the 18,000 he says will be affected. If we look at appendix C we find the different salary ranges comprise the following percentages of the classified service:

Not one civil servant in the classified service earns exactly $1,000 because there is no such category. The class salary range is $720, $780, $840, $900, $960 and then $1,020. The minister might have gone a little higher and put the cleavage where it should naturally have been, that is, at $1,020. Who gave him the information or advice or suggestion to
make the division at $1,000 when the nearest approach to that is $960 and then the salary jumps to $1,020?
It is true that the number of those who earn $1,020 and under is 2,145, but none of them earns exactly $1,000. There were 106 in the classified service at $960 or 721 earning up to that amount. If we take it that one-quarter of the classified service resides in Ottawa, then there would be 180 or at the very utmost 200 of them in this city who would be affected. That shows the fault or want of logic in making the division at $1,000 rather than at $1,020 where the cleavage should have been made.
Of those who earn from $720 to $960 there are about 200 in Ottawa and there may be about 700 in the whole of Canada. I do not think any of them are married, though undoubtedly some of those who earn that amount have certain dependents. Some may help their mother or brothers and sisters, but they are the very few. Why not, for instance, have started at the class, grade 2, getting $1,080 where, for example the letter carriers start, most of whom have dependents? The unfortunate feature of this attempted legislation is that it hits where it is least needed, but when the bill is in committee we will go more fully into that aspect of the situation.
Let us take the unclassified service and see how far we get within range of the 18,000 who in this time of stress are to be benefited by this most generous legislation. There are about 60,000 employees in the unclassified service. Uinder the prevailing rates there are some 6,000 and part-time, seasonal, postmasters, etcetera, about 18,000. Who are the people in this unclassified portion who would benefit? I am taking this from the Statistics of the Civil Service of Canada, numbers employed and expenditures on salaries by departments, published under the authority of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Let us take the Department of Agriculture first and move rapidly through the list. In that department the unclassified portion who would 'benefit are day labourers engaged in work necessitated principally in connection with experimental farms. In the Department of Immigration and Colonization the inspectors of immigration who are permanent officials of the Department of National Revenue, are paid part-time wages only and as has already been shown in customs returns, their part-time wages-from $50 to $400 per annum-paid by this department are included in salaries and wages of " non-enumerated classes."
Civil Service-Salary Deduction

In the Department of Labour the same thing applies. In the Department of Marine, the expenditure on wages for all ships' companies and casual help is included under "non-enumerated classes;" the latter includes the working force employed during the summer months in deepening and widening the St. Lawrence ship channel, also artisans and labourers employed by the day as required at the Sorel shipyard and on construction work. Is there something in the far distance or the near distance or what?
In the Department of Fisheries it includes wages for egg-sorters employed for short periods, and fishery guardians employed occasionally for short periods.
In the Department of National Defence, the members of the permanent naval, military and air forces are not regarded as civil servants. Hence neither numbers of personnel nor expenditures on pay are included in this report. Transient labour is sometimes employed by military engineers on repairs and construction work.
In the Department of National Revenue it is occasionally necessary to engage employees for a few hours or days at the most, yet these still appear as those who have benefited by this generous return.
In Pensions and National Health, in the health branch, where there is no part time salaried medical officer to look after sick sailors on landing at maritime ports, private practitioners give attention to these sailors and render their accounts to the department. Occasionally when a vessel having quarantin-able diseases on board arrives at a quarantine station it is necessary to engage a nurse or other help for a few days to assist the regular staff. These are among the eighteen thousand who will benefit.
In the Post Office, the employees of revenue post offices and sub post offices, together with mail contractors and licensed vendors are placed in the category of "non-enumerated classes." Mail contractors are paid under the tender and contract system, and as a rule do not give the whole of their time to the postal service. Most of the people affected by this disposition are people who have other avocations, they are not full time servants of the crown, they have some other means of livelihood, while those in the enumerated classes, the civil servants so-called, are by law precluded from engaging in any other sphere of activity than the service of the state. Those therefore are some who will be helped by the generosity of the government.

I have therefore shown that up to the present there might be in the city of Ottawa 180 in the unclassified, and probably some 600 to 650 charwomen. There are also classified temporaries not under the civil service commission, probably some 300, so that the total affected here will be from about 1,130 to 1,200. In all Canada there are 721 in thi3 class, grade one, with salary of $457,000; in Ottawa 180 with salary of about $114,000; 650 charwomen with wages of $22,650; and 300 unclassified at $900 or a total of $270,000. That is there would be altogether $406,952 upon which to draw this ten per cent. So this year the government would return probably $40,000, but from this one class alone they had during the last years over $80,000.
Now let us see the fairness of this return, in view of what the minister told the house when he presented his budget the other day. The total payroll of the classified service in Canada was $91,000,000 odd. The Ottawa payroll for the same period was $19,134,000 or twenty per cent of the salaries. The ten per cent deduction in 1931 gave $8,700,000. Ottawa contributed in cash $2,000,000. One quarter of about 8,000 statutory increases would amount to something like $250,000. The promotions that were stopped would represent something like $75,000. In other words, Ottawa has contributed $2,325,000. And Ottawa produced that amount out of $8,-. 700,000 or thirty per cent of the revenue with twenty per cent of the salaries paid.
But that is not all with reference to the treatment that these people are getting now. Take for instance a chief clerk in the service; his maximum is $3,720. Suppose he was at $3,480 when the ten per cent came. His present salary is $3,480. Ten per cent off is $348, the increase stopped, $240, the deductions therefore outside of his five per cent for superannuation amount to $588 or sixteen per cent, to which adding the five per cent gives twenty-one per cent instead of ten per cent. The straight deduction by the stopping of promotions and statutory increases and the ten per cent cut bring it to sixteen per cent.
Take another class, a head clerk, a similar calculation shows the result to be seventeen per cent. Yet when the minister spoke the other day he told the house that in the last two years they had taken in a phenomenal amount of money-I will come to that in a moment.
There is another feature about it. Who are those who will benefit? Following the rules

Civil Service-Salary Deduction
of the house I asked His Honour for some information in respect to the staff. I asked:
Are all the sessional staffs of the House of Commons to be benefited by the terms of the proposed Salary Deduction Act just introduced?
Answer: No.
Question: If not all, which ones will?
Answer: Charwomen, pages and parliamentary restaurant employees in receipt of salaries of $1,200 or less per annum.
Question: If any are excluded, which ones are they, what are the reasons therefor?
Answer:	Sessional clerks, protective staff,
messengers, servants, debates staff, stenographers.
As to the reasons, I am furnished with a circular letter number 115 dated April 11, 1934, from the office of the comptroller of the treasury. I do not know whether these regulations have been changed since; if they have, so much the better, they could not have been made worse than they are now. If they have not been changed, I shall cite them so that the minister may take cognizance of them and change them. Now what is the result? Take these two cases and see the logic of it. A stenographer here during the last session earned $690, at the rate of $5 a day. But for the purpose of this bill her salary must be computed at 365 days at $5, or equivalent to a yearly salary of $1,825, therefore she gets no benefit from the proposed restoration. A servant who last year worked, say, 300 days at $2.75, was paid $825. The government in its greed at the time of taxation takes the $825, taxes it $82.50, but this year when it is a question of returning it, they say to this man, you must calculate your salary at $2.75 a day for 365 days, and as the total remuneration so worked out comes to $1,003.75 he does not get back his ten per cent. That is based on this regulation, the fourth paragraph of the letter:
The bill is applicable to all employees, including prevailing rates, seasonal and sessional, and in order to establish whether the annual compensation will be above or below $1,000. accounting officers will establish what would be the amount earned if the employee were continuously employed for the full twelve months, and then treat the employee in accordance with the classification thus theoretically established.
When it comes down to returning the ten per cent, then all kinds of regulations are made so that the civil servants will not be able to get it back. But when it was a question of deducting, then if a man earned $16, or had been paid during the past year S35 for some small services he might have rendered, he was taxed $3.50. Then we are told by hon. members opposite that this is
a most generous move, and that the 18,000 people affected will to a considerable extent be benefited.
These deductions are made, in the face of a statement by the minister made on April 18, which is reported at page 2284, of Hansard, as follows:
To achieve this result, there has necessarily been a rigid scrutiny and control of departmental activities and personnel. From 1930 to 1933, government employees, including fluctuating as well as permanent staffs, were reduced by over 12,000 in number. The saving in salaries and wages exceeds $10,000,000 a year, not including the saving of some $7,800,000 arising out of the ten per cent salary deduction.
Mind you, Mr. Speaker, that from this particular class of service there has been a saving in salaries and wages exceeding $10,000,000 a year, outside of the sum of $7,800,000, and all this without one cent of expense for collection. Yet, when it comes to handing back some of this money we find exactly the contrary attitude. In other words the government took away from the service every penny it possibly could, and now when the time comes when they could do something, particularly in view of the tremendous amount of money they collected so easily, they deny even the most elementary rights of justice.
I could elaborate at greater length. What does the taking away of that amount of money from the civil servants amount to? It means that between the years 1930 and 1933, at a saving of $10,000,000 a year there has been a total saving of $30,000,000 in addition to the saving of $7,800,000 for a period of three years, amounting to $23,400,000, or a grand total of $53,400,000. There is that amount of money less in circulation among the civil service employees. One can readily imagine the amount of purchasing power which has been lost.
Next I should like to direct the attention of hon. members to the denial of promotions. This is one point which could not be considered in connection with the figures quoted by the minister. Mr. Speaker, before the second reading of this bill is adopted I think we are supposed to express our opinion in regard to the principle embodied in it. Lest the second reading should go by without very much protest, thereby conveying the impression that this chamber is almost unanimously in favour of this bill and the principle embodied therein, I feel like voicing my own opposition to the principle of the further continuance of the salary deduction.
We have had this salary deduction imposed on our civil service for the years 1932 and 1933, and on each of those occasions I took the privilege of speaking in favour of the principle. I did so for various reasons. I realized that the Finance minister had difficulty in meeting his obligations. Revenues were down, expenditures were increasing, and it was necessary to conserve in the expenditure of money in every way possible. Also I realized that throughout the country in general there was a tendency among business firms, commercial houses, agricultural people, school teachers and so on to reduce
salaries, and the government therefore was simply moving with the general tendency in the years 1932 and 1933.
But now, Mr. Speaker, conditions are somewhat different from what they were two years ago. Instead of business firms and commercial houses reducing salaries and having their employees get along on a lower wage scale, just the reverse is happening. We notice in the papers quite frequently items such as this one from Chemainus, B.C. This dispatch is dated February 28, 1934, and it says that nearly one thousand employees get a pay increase. The Victoria Lumber and Manufacturing Company have given their employees a wage increase of approximately ten per cent, effective March 1. I have another clipping here from Toronto, that the Toronto board of education has decided against any salary reduction in 1934, and has restored to the teachers the five per cent reduction that was in effect during the last two years.
Also another clipping to the effect that the United States Senate overrode administration forces and voted to restore one-third of the federal pay cut of last February and to give back the full fifteen per cent reduction effective July 1. And so on. I could quote a number of similar extracts showing that there is a general tendency to restore that which has been taken away for the past couple of years.
It seems to me that the dominion government will be moving along the right line if they too decide to restore that which has been kept back from the civil service for the past two years. I realize that they are making a slight gesture in that direction, but it is so slight that it is very difficult even to see it, and the benefits accruing therefrom are not going to be very extensive. It would seem to me that if the entire salary cut were restored to the civil service, while it would mean the raising of an additional $8,000,000, yet the benefits to be derived from putting that amount of money into circulation would be felt in a great many channels throughout the country, including the channels of taxation. It would mean, for example, that the returns from the sales tax would be considerably increased; it would mean that the income tax returns would also be increased. It would mean that business in general throughout the dominion would receive such a stimulus that it is quite likely that a considerable portion of the additional $8,000,000 expended would come back into the dominion treasury before the end of the year.

But in any case, even though it did not, I note in Hansard that the minister in his budget address tells us that he anticipates revenue for the ensuing year to exceed expenditure by the amount of $8,800,000. That being the ease, even though there should be no revenue at all come back because of this $8,000,000 of additional expenditure, there would yet be $800,000 of a surplus, according to the minister's own figures.
Another point I would like to put before the minister is this. The government of the day has penalized the civil service of this country for two years by subjecting the civil service to' a ten per cent reduction. But the wages of money have not yet been penalized. The largest item in our estimates is made up of interest on our public debt, $141,494,853.65 being the interest for the ensuing year. Without going into the question whether the government is competent legally to take action in regard to interest reduction, although I realize that Australia has taken action and reduced her interest charges by 22J per cent, I would point out that if the government did take action and reduced interest charges by ten per cent, so that a levy was put on the wages of money, as well as having a levy put for the past two years on the wages of hard-working civil servants -if we put such a levy on the interest accumulating on our national debt it would bring us in over fourteen million dollars in one year. I would commend to the minister, if he feels that he must have this additional money, the taking of action along the line of reducing the wages of money, which is interest, and restoring to the hard-working civil servants that which I am sure they will be glad to receive, and if they receive it I am sure they will put it into circulation by spending it properly.

speechtext:
My colleague the senior member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) who has just spoken, is recognized, I think, in this house as an authority on civil service matters, and therefore I do not propose to elaborate on the civil service statistics that he has presented to the house.
When the salary deduction bill of two years ago was ' introduced I stated that in my opinion such a bill was a wide open invitation to business to discharge employees and cut salaries. I think the same thing applies today. The businessmen of the country follow the lead of the government; the government is a barometer to business and industry. Public employees were being discharged, retirements were being hastened and salaries were cut and the employers observed that

barometer and tightened their belts. Up to that time many employers had felt that they were doing a patriotic duty by trying to maintain wages and keep employees at work but the government legislation gave them a definite lead. I believe this action of the government is simply a vote of want of confidence in its own fiscal policy; it is simply a matter of deflation, of tightening the belt and it has been followed throughout the country. It is a strange paradox to see the government causing unemployment and the lowering of wages on the one hand and paying out huge sums of moneys for relief with the other. I think the condition of our revenues to-day can be blamed on the basic policies of this government. Towering tariff walls and extreme deflation all along the line must lead inevitably to a burden of direct taxation. The present policy is not different from what it was in 1930.
I think hon. members will realize that the civil service is what might be described as Ottawa's most important industry. It employs the greatest number of men and women and the wages and salaries paid are more than those paid by all other industries combined. The purchasing power of the city depends upon the civil service. When the dismissals occurred, followed by the ten per cent cut and the loss of the statutory increases, a terrific blowWas dealt to this city. I do not believe the people throughout the country realize what a concentrated blow was dealt to one particular community. The effect of the dismissals and the cut in salaries was immediately felt in Ottawa. The earnings of practically all business concerns began to fall and many were forced to follow the government's example. Where three persons had been employed in a grocery store, let us say, one was let out and as a rule the two kept on suffered some reduction in pay. Business failures became quite prevalent. I know, from my own experience, that many Ottawa businessmen are simply hanging on by their finger nails. A large departmental store which was founded by men who had played a big part in the building up of this city and whose memory is still fresh in the minds of most of the people of Ottawa went into receivership. The irony of it all is that this was caused by a government whose election promise was employment for all.
Last January the number of heads of families on direct relief in Ottawa was 5,000. The census of 1930 gives Ottawa a population of only 130,000. Those in charge of the relief situation in Ottawa tell me that there are still

Civil Service-Salary Deduction
about 4,700 heads of families on direct relief. There are also many unemployed persons being taken care of by relatives, while the missions and hostels are full of single men. The welfare bureau estimates five to a family, so hon. members will see that the unemployment situation in this city has assumed very serious proportions. I think any businessman in Ottawa will admit that the problem with respect to unoccupied houses, shops and apartments is becoming very grave.
If the reports in the press are true that employment is increasing in Canada, I am afraid Ottawa has lagged far behind. Optimistic reports have appeared in the press and optimistic statements have been made by members of the ministry in connection with the rise in revenues and I do not think anything else has received as much attention from my constituents. They feel that if these things are true, then they should receive some relief. However, I am afraid their hopes have been blasted. That seems to be the only definite policy of the government, to blast the hopes of the people of this country.
In these days of disappointments, we must be thankful for small mercies, and the return of the salary deduction of ten per cent to certain employees-I understand they number about 1,200 of whom about 700 are charwomen-is a matter of real satisfaction to the people of this city. Perhaps these people needed it the most, but the fact remains that this bill does not benefit the real civil service of the country. I understand that in Ottawa there are about 10,500 people who will not be affected by the provisions of this bill. These are the people who are charged with the main responsibility of carrying on the varied activities of government, but this great body of men and women receive no relief by the removal of the salary deduction or the restoration of the statutory increases. I warn the government, in all seriousness, that its policies with respect to the civil service are beginning to undermine the morale of the service as a whole. The service is beginning to feel that the present government has no sympathy for it or for those who live in the capital of Canada. Faith and hope are becoming seriously undermined in Ottawa. The minister tells the civil service to go on hoping. Now the civil service of Canada, as I think all hon. members of this house will agree, are an exceptionally fine body of men and women and they have exceptionally fine and high traditions of service. I remember, and I think hon. gentlemen will also recollect, the statement made by the Right Hon. Stanley Baldwin in which he expressed words of high 74726-165
appreciation of those civil servants of Canada with whom he had come in contact, and, coming from a country where the civil service stands very high in the esteem of the people, he paid the civil service of Canada, I think, a great compliment. After dashing to the ground the hopes of the civil service, the Minister of Finance, speaking on the budget, made the following statement as reported at page 2293 of Hansard:
At the same time, while the improvement has been gradual, it has not only been sustained but has progressively increased. This is evidenced by the splendid increases in both imports and exports for the month of March, which show a proportionate advance in volume of trade hitherto unprecedented.
It is generally recognized that this depression and its blighting effects have been world wide. This fact of itself has had the tendency to produce a "depression psychology," followed by what might be termed a "depression weariness." The result is that we do not so readily recognize and properly appraise the incontrovertible evidences of reviving activity which have made their appearance.
These signs of improvements are so marked as to indicate beyond question that we are on the road to recovery. May we with renewed hope, fresh courage and firm step

I wonder who wrote that.
-press on towards the goal of better and happier days which lie not far ahead.
The minister is certainly optimistic and full of hope, and I cannot help feeling, as I am sure most other people feel, that he might have done somewhat better in this matter of salary restoration. He plainly voices a hope there, but he is not willing to take a chance of any kind. I understand that the revenues of the country in April have improved to a marked degree.
The policy of our neighbours in the United States has been to raise the wage levels and to reduce unemployment, but by a strange paradox this policy did not provide for the restoration of salary reductions to the civil service, which I understood amounted to 15 per cent. So that the Senate of the United States, no doubt realizing that this was inconsistent with a recovery program, have passed, over the president's veto, an act which provides for the full restoration of the 15 per cent by next July. An extremely cautious chancellor of the exchequer has also restored half of the reduction to the civil service of Great (Britain. It seems, therefore, that the legislatures of Great Britain and the United States appreciate their respective civil services rather more than we do ours in Canada. Personally, I think that if there had been only a restoration of say half the cuts it would have caused great satisfaction in this

country and1 would have stimulated business men. They would have felt that things were on the upgrade, and that the government was leading the way in the restoration of higher wage levels and greater employment.
I cannot help regretting that the minister, who has one of the kindest hearts in this house, did not feel himself able to do something substantial for a 'body of people who have suffered severely during the last two or three years. People generally forget, and perhaps hon. members in this house do, that during the boom years, 1927, 1928 and 1929, the wage increases to those engaged in industry generally reached a point 90 per cent above the figures of 1913, while those of civil servants went up to only 60 per cent. If civil service salaries do not keep pace with those paid in general industry, can the people of Ottawa be blamed for coming more and more to the conclusion that the government is not really in sympathy with the civil service and the people who live here?
Let me take the example afforded by the order in council brought down by the Secretary of State a few years ago, providing ' that no civil servant may run for the city council or the board of control without the permission of the head of the department. Consider the number of civil servants entitled to vote in municipal elections in Ottawa. They are wanted in the city council of Ottawa because they naturally represent a very large cross-section of the city and of Ottawa public opinion. Let us suppose that a large industry pursued the same policy; I think a roar of disapproval would go up. I would suggest that that order in council be rescinded.
An election is being indefinitely delayed, and the people of Canada are voting no confidence in the government. Now public opinion must be heeded by public men. I commend Canadian history to those who doubt that statement. I commend them to look at what happened to the government of Alexander Mackenzie who remained in office a little too long; I understand that the Liberal party was out for about twenty years. And Sir Charles Tupper also disregarded byelection results, and we all know that the Conservative party was out of office fifteen years. It can be seen, I think, that history has a marvelous way of repeating itself. I commend that thought to members of the present government
I rather hope that the present government does stay in one year longer than the ordinary life of parliament, because the public will know how to deal with those who will not

respect popular opinion. Let them stay in, praying for the backwash of Roosevelt and British prosperity; but the people will exact the penalty all the same. History teaches that.
In the next election campaign the Prime Minister, I suppose, will address an audience in Ottawa, and I shall not be surprised or shocked if the audience at that meeting forms itself into a giant glee club and sings at the conclusion of his address:
It is all very well to dissemble your love,
But why did you kick us downstairs?

remember correctly. When this salary deduction legislation was originally passed I understood it was to be for just a year and of course we have had a reiteration of that policy from year to year since the act was first passed. We have now the spectacle where the government comes to the house in a spirit of contrition and the amount of money that is going to be returned to the civil service is about two per cent of the original cut. I was pleased to-day to see the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) also in a spirit of contrition. We are gradually winning over all those who thought the soundest way to get out of the depression was by decreasing wages. Now we see the general movement toward what I consider the sound stand adopted by the forces of labour in this country in connection with wages. Whether we like it or not, the salaries paid constitute the cornerstone of the business life of the dominion. That has been recognized in every country in the world. It has been recognized in part by the institution of a committee under the jurisdiction of the government. It has been recognized by the republic to the south of us. It has been recognized by the government of Great

Britain in giving back to their civil servants some part of the deductions made in their salaries. It has been recognized by the railroads of the United States. I notice in today's paper that the ten per cent deduction placed in operation there is going to be returned completely to the men during the next year. It has also been recognized by the government of Ontario; whether on the basis of pure economics or politics, I would not like to say. Nevertheless they in their wisdom find that the soundest way of bringing that province and, of course, this country in turn, back on an even keel is by a restitution of the reduction of wages put into operation by them.
I would like to have seen the federal government go further. I do not say that for political effect; it is a position I have always taken, a position the labour movement in this and every other country has taken in connection with wages of men and women not only in the civil service but also in industrial and business pursuits. Until we find a way of permitting the people to consume the things they produce, we shall never get out of the wrnods and that is true not only of this but of every other country. The present recommendation of the government does not go far enough; it includes 18,000 civil servants who receive wages below $1,000 per annum and I understand it affects only two per cent of the permanent service.
I would like to make one or two suggestions to the minister particularly in regard to temporary employees, and especially stenographers. I understand their salaries are based on a daily wage and of course they will not come within the confines of this legislation. I believe they should be treated just the same as some of the more highly paid officials of the government whose duties to a large degree centre around the sessions of parliament. It would be a constructive policy that rather than those girls being paid just for the five or six months they are here, they should be granted an annual salary and possibly allowed to come within the jurisdiction of the 'Civil Service Commission. I think it is fair to say that most of them, when they leave here, are more or less kept in idleness until the next session of parliament rolls around. I am not saying this in criticism of the conditions enjoyed by those higher officials of the house whom I have mentioned.
Further, I do not think the bill goes far enough. Many of the employees coming within the provisions of the bill are single. If they are not single; if the argument should be that many of them are married, I would suggest as I have done before that their wage 74726-165J
rates be investigated by the Stevens committee now considering the question of sweated labour. It would be well if the government would seriously consider this matter.
It is passing strange to see how the mental outlook of human beings goes in cycles. We get the cycle where people think the solution to the problem is through cutting wages. May I make this observation: if that is a solution to the problem, then let us work for nothing and we shall all become rich. If low wages and intolerable conditions constitute the basis of the success of any country, China and India would be the most successful in the world. I wish to add a few words to the protest that has been made by other members on this side of the house in connection with this bill. Like the others I am of course in favour of the bill in so far as it restores some of the deductions that have been made in former years. But I believe the government could have gone considerably further in restoring the deductions to the lower grades. I'believe when the bill came up in 1932 some members on this side, possibly of this group, proposed an amendment that the deductions should not apply to any salary or wage less than $1,800 a year. I believe that $1,800 enables a family, if it is not too large, to have a fairly decent standard of living, though not at all commensurate with what we could have in this country if we had proper distribution and were allowed to produce wealth in the way and to the amount that we could. So I suggest to the minister and the government even now that, as they feel that conditions are improving and that there has been some gain since the date on which the announcement was made and the bill introduced in the house, they should consider increasing the number of exemptions in the bill.
Before I say anything more, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) upon the position he has taken to-day. I remember last year when I spoke along similar lines he censured me rather severely, which hurt me somewhat, and which I rather resented at the time, because I pointed out then that I was not seeking an increase for myself, that I would have even agreed to have my own indemnity still further reduced if thereby those who were getting lower wages could have their salaries increased or could be exempted from the deduction. I am glad to-day to see that he has come to realize that, as I think the hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mitchell) said, we cannot bring back prosperity by reducing wages.
Another effect of the salary deduction bill is that it has eliminated the annual increments resulting from promotions from one grade to another. This also is a hardship, and I do not think it is right that it should continue. I also wish to point out that the government itself is violating the terms of the bill by discriminating between individuals in the

civil service. I have before me copies of various orders in council that have been passed recently increasing salaries. There is one case of an inspector in the income tax office for Montreal district who had his salary increased from $4,500 to $5,800. I think when a person is receiving a salary of $4,500 a year he is suffering no great hardship, that he can live fairly decently on that. Yet we have the government, that refuses to increase the salary of stenographers who receive a very small wage, or continues to reduce the wages of others who receive more than $1,000 a year, increasing the salary of a person who is already receiving the relatively high salary of $4,500 a year. There is another, an assistant inspector of income tax at the Montreal office, whose salary has been increased from $2,800 to $4,000 under authority of order in council. Another one, a clerk, grade one, raised to grade two. Another, a clerk, grade one, promoted to grade three, an increase of wages going with all of these promotions. Rather than discriminate in this manner, I think it would be much better for the government to restore altogether the deductions that have been made and bring harmony and contentment into the civil service. I believe that we are all becoming convinced now that the great problem before the world, and the problem that is facing this dominion, is to find some means to distribute the wealth that we can produce in such great abundance. I am quite satisfied that we can never do that by decreasing the medium through which the individuals draw upon that wealth.
In my opinion the government should be a model employer. They should set an example to other employers. That does not mean being extravagant or wasteful. They should first set a remuneration sufficient to provide a certain standard of living, and then see that no one in their employ receives less than that remuneration. I say again that the government would be wise, they would be doing a good thing for this country by restoring all the deductions made in 1932, or, as a minimum, by exempting from the bill all employees receiving less than $2,000 a year.

subtopic: SALARY DEDUCTION ACT-RESTORATION OF TEN PER CENT CUT TO EMPLOYEES RECEIVING $1,000 OR LESS
speechtext:
To
begin with a minor matter, I think there must be some misunderstanding in the minds of many hon. members of the house and of the sessional staff in connection with the staff's remuneration or the deduction. A pay day has passed since the minister announced that the ten per cent would be restored in

Civil Service-Salary Deduction
part, and the staff has had no restoration. Apparently for that reason they think they are not going to get any. Take the question of the stenographers who get around $150 a month, which is figured as $1,800 a year. That being over $1,000, the department has ruled that they cannot get the ten per cent restored. But I do not see how the government can possibly evade-I do not believe they want to-the terms of the bill that:
no provision of this act shall operate to reduce the compensation of any member of the public service of Canada below one thousand dollars per annum.
If it be found at the end of the year that members of this staff have not earned $1,000 in the year I suggest that it is very much up to the government to give them back the ten per cent for the limited portion of the year which they have worked, even though at the time they were working at a rate' greater than one thousand dollars a year. That seems only reasonable. I trust the minister will take steps, either by regulation or perhaps by an explanation in committee, to make that clear. I wish he would do so, because there is a great deal of misunderstanding not only among hon. members but also among people to whom this matter is one of great concern.
I wish to touch upon another method of accounting, which I think is unfair. Seamen on government boats receive very small pay -I believe it is $65 a month-and board. The government have a habit of putting a fictitious valuation, inasmuch as it is a sum arranged by themselves, on the value of the board the seamen receive. That amount is added to the $65, with the result that the total is brought to a point where the ten per cent may be deducted. These men are not given very much in cash. They are given the food the government buys for them, which is bought at a price the government purchaser thinks best. Whether or not the buying is done in the most economic way, we do not know and the men concerned have no say in the matter. They are charged with a certain sum-and I forget whether it is $25 or $35 per month-but at least an arbitrary sum which is reckoned as part of their wages. Many of the men are married and have to maintain homes on land. It is notorious that a man living with his family can live far cheaper than when living by himself. Surely that is a matter which should be taken into consideration. For instance, if a department sends a permanent official from Ottawa out to the Pacific coast or to any other point in the dominion on public business, the whole of his expenses are paid while
such official is away. Bills for hotel accommodation, board, and other necessary expenditures are paid. Those men are not charged with the board expenses, nor is the ten per cent deduction taken on the additional amount. Such computation would not be reasonable.
The next thing I would expect to hear- and I am afraid to make the suggestion for fear the minister should grasp at it-is that the men would be charged for their sleeping accommodation, blankets and' so on. Although this may be a matter of small concern to most people in the dominion, it is of great concern to the men directly interested. I know of my own personal knowledge that it does make a very great difference. Taking the ten per cent from a man who is receiving only $65 in cash for the support of his wife, his home and his children, acts as a severe strain on his resources.
To some extent I should like to follow the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Maclnnis). I suggest that as times are improving, and as in every return, national revenues are increasing, the minister might consider whether in months to come, possibly in a period of six months from the beginning of the fiscal year, he could reconsider the situation, and just now make the necessary provision in the act. If at that time he found conditions had improved sufficiently, instead of waiting another six months he could then restore the ten per cent cut in its entirety. In my view he might very well do that. Such procedure would not cost him any money if the revenue was not coming in as fast as he thought it should be to justify a further increase. The minister himself showed an indication of his views in this connection because, as a matter of fact, he hesitated to make a decision in regard to the reductions until he had before him the last possible returns so as to ascertain what action would be justified.
At this point I shall deal with the bill in its wider aspects, and first congratulate the Minister of Finance upon his courage in bringing down that which he must know is an unpopular measure. With an election in sight he must realize that in the larger cities or those points of the dominion where civil servants predominate, the measure will not be received kindly. It could not have been his own disposition to incur all the odium involved, unless he considered his action entirely necessary. For that and other reasons I shall vote for the second reading of the bill. I do suggest however that he should have made the minimum limit greater, and in committee

Civil Service-Salary Deduction
ment and the civil service commission classify the office and the postmaster begins at a minimum salary of $2,040, with increases of S60 a year up to the maximum of $2,400. The assistants who previous to his obtaining that classification were paid by him out of the bulk revenue of the office are no longer paid in that way. They become regular civil servants and their salaries are fixed by the civil service commission according to the classification of the post office in which they are working. The classification may give them $700, $750 or $900, and the postmaster has nothing at all to do with the fixing of their remuneration. The postmaster in the class B-2 post office becomes a regular civil servant. He suffers the salary deduction of ten per cent, say $200. But if he had not become a regular civil servant, if he remained under the old classification of his office, his deduction would have amounted to $400 or $500. In this way an injustice is done. The regular civil servant has suffered only a reduction in his salary which is fixed by the commission but the country postmaster has had to suffer a reduction in loss of revenue and a reduction in salary. If the revenues of the post office had kept up to the 1930 figure the injustice done would not have been so great, but I think it will be found that the revenues of a post office, especially of these commission offices, has been reduced considerably. I believe there is a difference of about $2,125,000 between the present revenues of the Post Office Department and what they were in 1930. I wish the minister would consider this matter and take it up with the officials of the Post Office Department.
I hold in my hand a copy of a memorial sent to the Post Office Department by the Canadian Postmasters' Association setting forth certain reasons why these things should be changed. I have given some of these reasons already and have added others. It cannot be said that this matter has not been brought to the attention of the government because the postmasters association has been very persistent in pointing out this injustice. When we were considering the bill which made a general reduction without any exception, I stated that I could not see how injustice could possibly be avoided.
There is certain information I should like to get when the bill is in committee. I do not oppose the second reading because we must be thankful for small mercies. The government has seen fit to make a readjustment up to a certain figure and while that does not meet my views in all respects, it is something. 
I understand that some 18,000 servants-I am not going to call them civil servants-of the government will be affected by this measure. I am distinguishing between civil servants and workers outside of what is really known as the civil service, especially those workers who do not come under the civil service commission for appointment or dismissal. I should like to know how many revenue and nonrevenue offices, that is accounting and nonaccounting offices, will be affected by this measure. With the aid of the Postmaster General's report I have endeavoured to arrive at the number of non-accounting offices, and I find there are some 3,000. I think I am pretty close to the correct figure. These nonaccounting offices are little country post offices in which the postmaster receives a salary of $100 per year. Previous to your humble servant occupying the position of Postmaster General in the former government, these postmasters received $60 per year. I increased this salary and I might say that that increase was strongly supported by the opposition of that day, the present government. The increases in these salaries and in connection with other offices amounted to over $1,000,000 in that year. But the present government has cut down these small, measly salaries. People will say that that does not make any difference, that this is ready-found money for these people as they are not dependent upon the salary for their living. That may be quite true but it must be remembered that they must give time to the work. There are many country post offices where the mails are received daily and although the revenue and the quantity of mail handled is small the postmaster or postmistress must attend to see that the mail is received and distributed. The postmaster cannot afford and the government cannot afford to have a separate building, and the postmaster uses his own house as the office. The government has done what I consider it had no right to do, cut down the rental allowance by ten per cent. A country postmaster may receive perhaps $20 per year for the use of his house but that has been cut by ten per cent. There are cases where the Post Office Department will not agree to a rental above $50 per year. Sometimes an application is made to the Department of Public Works and rather than undertake the construction of a public building to be used as a post office, that department will add $50 more for rental.
Not only was that allowance cut, but the allowance for night work was cut. Under our laws a country post office need not keep

Civil Service-Salary Deduction
open after eight o'clock at night but any postmaster in a small country post office will tell you that people come in at eight, nine, ten, eleven and even twelve o'clock to get their mail. They come in from long distances and they see a light in the house and they come and ask for their mail. It has always been a question whether night service of that kind should be paid for by the department, but it was recognized in many cases. It does not amount to very much and is a help to the postmaster, and yet that night allowance is cut.
I am not going to ask the minister to look into too many things but I do ask him to look into the reduction in the rental, forwarding and night allowances. I ask him to see if some rectification cannot be made of what I claim to be injustices. From my experience as head of the department I know they are injustices. These injustices have existed for two years, which is too long. I hold the minister to the promise he made me when I withdrew my objection to the second reading of the bill last year, that any injustice which could be shown would be rectified. I feel quite sure the Post Office Department will admit that these are injustices and if they will not admit that, I should like to discuss them upon the floor of this house.
Mr .W. A. BEYNON (Moose Jaw): I do not wish to delay the house for any length of time on this bill. I do wish however to associate myself to some extent with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). It is not very often that we see eye to eye, but on this occasion I think he was quite sound when he said that in discussing this bill we are not discussing wages in Canada but are discussing the private business of the government of this country. And I believe he was quite sound also when he said that a government cannot spend itself rich any more than an individual can. I know that an individual cannot because I have tried it.
I cannot be at all surprised that the members representing the city of Ottawa should take the stand that they have taken on this bill. I can quite appreciate their being in favour of restoring the cut to the civil service of the country. I was however a little surprised at the attitude taken by the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael). It seemed to back up to some extent the stand taken by the junior member for Ottawa. He referred to the fact that business concerns in this city had gone bankrupt, and that was partly due to the reduction in the salaries of civil servants in the city. I want to say that the
city of Ottawa does not know anything about depression. That is the situation.

subtopic: SALARY DEDUCTION ACT-RESTORATION OF TEN PER CENT CUT TO EMPLOYEES RECEIVING $1,000 OR LESS
speechtext:
Would that be a reason for inflicting this on Ottawa?
Mr. BEYN'ON:	It is a reason why the
people of the rest of Canada who are really suffering a depression and know what it means should not have to pay the additional taxation necessary to restore the cut. That is what it means, and I agree with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni when he says he could not support the restoration of the cut and go back to his constituents, who are suffering a decrease in revenue not comparable at all with the slight decrease which the civil servants have received, but infinitely greater, in some instances their revenue having been absolutely wiped out, and in other eases having slight revenues but being taxed to the limit of their capacity to pay the taxes of the country.
Then we have as a necessary measure one-half of the original tax on sugar. I will not stand up in this house and recommend returning the whole of the civil service cut until that tax is removed and until the revenues of the country will warrant its removal, because that is being borne by the whole of the people of Canada, who can much less afford it than the civil servants can afford to suffer this small cut.
People coming from western Canada to the city of Ottawa are struck by the fact that the people of Ottawa do not know the first thing about depression. The member for Kindersley is fully aware of that. He is a gentleman for whose views I have a great deal of respect and he is usually very sound, but I think he got off the trail this afternoon. I should like to see the salaries returned to civil servants. It is not that I have the slightest thing against the civil service and I should like to see them have the cut restored. But they are much better off, even with the reduction, than ninety-five per cent of the people of the west who are paying taxes to pay the salaries. That is the situation, and while that obtains I do not feel that I could stand in this house and advocate the return of the cut.
The hon. member for Kindersley spoke about taxing the wages of money. That subject has been explored, and he frankly admitted that he could not suggest how it could be done. I should like to see it done, and to a certain extent it is being done in so far as the refunding has been reducing interest. So far as the government is able to do that, they are doing it to their utmost.

Civil Service-Salary Deduction
There is one respect in which I wish to associate myself with the senior member for Ottawa, and that is with regard to the salaries of the sessional staff, those who are receiving as a matter of fact much less than one thousand a year because they are employed only during the term of the session. I do not think it is sound to compute their salary on the assumption that if employed all year they would receive over $1,000, because we know as a matter of fact that they are employed only a few months, less than half the year, and some of them come long distances. They are not overpaid. Those who have come since the increases were stopped get only $4 a day, and after they have paid their expenses they have little left. I hope the minister will give that consideration and that it can be adjusted.
I have also some sympathy with the arguments of the ex-Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot). I know there are some postmasters in the revenue post offices who should receive consideration at the hands of the minister. While I am not as familiar with that subject as the ex-Postmaster General is, I know that there is hardship. How the matter can be adjusted I do not know but I am sure the minister will give it his attention.
That is all I wish to say on the subject. I have nothing in the world against the civil service or against their getting their pay back, but while the hardly-pressed people of the west are suffering hardships, while they are in that plight, I do not feel that I could stand in this house and ask that the reductions be restored.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SALARY DEDUCTION ACT-RESTORATION OF TEN PER CENT CUT TO EMPLOYEES RECEIVING $1,000 OR LESS
speechtext:
I do not propose to take the time of the house for more than a few moments, especially as it will be more convenient, in committee of the w'hole, to deal with many of the individual and specific matters raised by different hon. members. I hope they wall realize that if I make no reference to any specific instance they have brought up I shall be glad to do so when we are in committee.
There are however one or two general observations, as touching upon the principle of the bill, on which I wish to say a few words, as a reaction from some of the remarks made by certain hon. members. Take the hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mitchell). He may be surprised to hear me say that I have always been an advocate of high wages. You show me the country where you have high wages and high prices and I will show you a country in which there are far more prosperous conditions than there are in the

country that has low wages and low prices. That is axiomatic. But my hon. friend goes off the rails, if I may use the vernacular, when he confuses wages with the amount paid to civil servants, which must come out of the pockets of the taxpayers, including the wage earners of the country.
My hon. friend from Comox-Alberni has suggested that it must be an unpleasant task for me to be associated with a measure of this kind. I assure him it is one of the most unpleasant duties I have ever had to discharge, and I have had many in my public life. But it is a duty, and one must perform one's duty. In that connection let me make this observation and I do it in all kindliness -with respect to a remark made by the junior member for Ottawa (Mr. Ahearn) when he referred to the ill fate that befell the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie who was recognized as having been such an honest man that he said he had to sleep on the public chest with arms beside him to protect it against the raids of divers and sundry people. I do not profess to be a prophet, but I venture the opinion we are coming to the time in this country when men of the character of Alexander Mackenzie are going to receive a far greater degree of veneration than they did in times past. This dominion is strewn with wreckage in the form of public expenditures running into the tens and hundreds of millions of dollars which have been made with the acclaim of the people, not realizing, poor souls, that the day would come when they would be called upon to pay the bills. That day has arrived in very large measure and there is on the part of the Canadian people a consciousness toward public expenditures, the like of which has not obtained before. I hope the junior member for Ottawa does not continue along the trail indicated by the process of thought he showed here to-day, because if he does so, I venture to say that his continuance in public life will not be long. He was enunciating the theory that we should, to put the matter baldly, purchase the people with their own money. He had in mind the fact that in times past spending governments were popular governments. That was true, but, as I say, that was in the days when people did not stop to think and realize they would ultimately be called upon to foot the bills. I do not want to indulge in any heroics but my mind recalls a statement of Abraham Lincoln when he said: "I would rather be right than be president." I may say to the junior member for Ottawa that I would rather do my duty as

Civil Service-Salary Deduction
I see it than be Prime Minister of Canada, even if that involves the protection of the people as against themselves. That leads me to say this: In the first place the hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mitchell), and some other hon. members for whose opinions I have the highest respect, fail utterly to take into consideration the fact that we are passing through a period the like of which has not hitherto been known in the history of the world. The very world is rocking and we are coping with a condition which we cannot measure or deal with on the basis on which we would have dealt with it under what we knew in times past as normal conditions.
The hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) for whose opinions, always formed as a matter of honest conviction, I have the highest respect, has fallen into error, I am afraid, when he suggests that by restoring the civil servants' pay we would improve conditions because we would be putting that much more money into circulation. I submit that we do no such thing. All we do is transfer from the pockets of all the taxpayers of Canada the $7,800,000 which would be required to be placed in the pockets of the civil servants who would receive that sum. You would increase the spending power of the civil servants to that extent but you would also diminish the purchasing power of the taxpayers to the same extent, and you are just as far ahead in the last analysis as you are in the first. The hon. member referred to the fact that an industry in British Columbia employing about a thousand men had restored the pay of its employees. Certainly, and why did they do that? Because they had the money with which to do it; the industry was earning sufficient to do it. The hon. member for Kindersley-and I hope he will not take exception to my singling him out for the moment because I want to deal with one or two of the arguments he put forward-said that the Minister of Finance in his budget estimated that we would have a surplus of some $8,000,000 during the coming year. That is true, but my hon. friend must bear in mind one or two factors. In the first place, as I know to my sorrow, this is a very difficult period in which to budget and we must have some margin of leeway. We are not dealing with budgets in the old days when conditions were more or less static. Last year I budgeted for a balanced budget this year, but I found I was wrong to the extent of $24,100,000, although I budgeted on the best advice which I could receive. There is not a country in the world which has not had that same difficulty in recent years. Let me point this out to the hon. member for
Kindersley and to the house: he did not refer to the matter, but several hon. members referred to the action of the British government in restoring a portion of the salary deductions of civil servants and others in Great Britain. In Great Britain they had a surplus, not on current account but on all accounts, of a stupendous sum, greater than the amount which we shall have added to our national debt for last year and this year. Notwithstanding that surplus, what did they do? They restored only one-half of the salary deduction, and these deductions applied to school teachers to the extent of fifteen per cent, policemen, judges, members of the defence forces, cabinet ministers, members of parliament, in some instances going to twenty per cent in the higher brackets and ten per cent in the lower.
Look at the picture in Canada in the light of what they did in Great Britain. Notwithstanding that huge surplus, the British government restored only a portion of the salary deduction. Why? Because they wanted to err on the side of caution, I presume. But in Canada all we are hoping to do this year is to balance the budget on current account and go into debt still further to the extent that we have to utilize funds to meet deficits on the Canadian National Railways, capital expenditures which are not taken care of out of revenue and the amount required for unemployment relief.
It may be a surprise to the two Ottawa members that I am just as anxious as they are to see the salary deductions restored, but as a public servant I have a duty to perform and I have to keep in mind the taxpayers of this country and the fact that we must maintain the credit and integrity of the dominion We would be far better off to inconvenience, if I may use that word as a milder term, those members of the civil service who have to make the sacrifice for another year-and I hope it is the last one-than we would if we dashed into a restoration of salaries, knowing that we could bring it about only through putting additional taxation on the people.

speechtext: Might I ask the minister this? I appreciate his words, but in view of what he said, would he remember, when the time comes, the burdens the civil service has borne?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SALARY DEDUCTION ACT-RESTORATION OF TEN PER CENT CUT TO EMPLOYEES RECEIVING $1,000 OR LESS
speechtext:
I yield to no man in this country in my appreciation of, in the main, the character of the work that is performed by the civil service. There are in the civil service the drones, as you will find in any large organization: there are some who are not earning one-tenth of their salary, but by and

Civil Service-Salary Deduction
large the civil service are as fine a body of public servants as you will find in any country in the world. They work long hours, and this country is extremely well served. In my experience and contact with them the latter class are the ones who complain least about this salary deduction, because they know the extremity in which the country is placed, and the dire necessity which forces the government to effect this saving.
I do not want to enter into a dissertation on economics or sociology, much less discuss the tariff, but I think it is necessary to make just one brief reference, because my hon. friend the junior member for Ottawa (Mr. Ahearn) was at pains to repeat what he had heard so many of his elders on the opposition side say, namely that our difficulties are due to the tariff policy of this government. He is a promising young man; I have every hope of his going far in public life and I do not want him to start off on the wrong foot, therefore I would warn him not to repeat in parrot fashion what he hears so frequently, or he may in time come to believe it himself. In the first place I never could understand what difference it makes to the taxpayers whether they pay by direct taxation or indirectly through the customs house. If you collect $100,000,000 in revenue through the customs house it comes out of the pockets of the people just as if it were collected in direct taxation.

subtopic: SALARY DEDUCTION ACT-RESTORATION OF TEN PER CENT CUT TO EMPLOYEES RECEIVING $1,000 OR LESS
speechtext: You would do more business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SALARY DEDUCTION ACT-RESTORATION OF TEN PER CENT CUT TO EMPLOYEES RECEIVING $1,000 OR LESS
speechtext:
I am prepared to admit that there are cases where the incidence is split; in some cases perhaps more is paid by the importer, in many cases it is paid by the exporter, and in some cases it is divided. But the point is that money expended by the people comes out of the pocket of someone, whether it comes through the customs house or through direct taxation. Let me point out to the junior member for Ottawa that we are not the only foolish people on earth. He cannot point to a single country in the world to-day, unless it be Russia, where there is no unemployment, and I am sure he would not want us to adopt the methods they employ there in order to avoid it. But let us say that the question he has raised in that regard is a matter which is open to argument. Well and good; we can discuss it in its proper time and place. But we are confronted with a condition and have to deal with it the best way we can, in the light of the ability of the taxpayers to meet their obligations.

One other thing, though perhaps this is hardly necessary in view of some remarks I have already made. My hon. friend the junior member for Ottawa said in plain terms that the feeling was growing that this government was out of sympathy with the civil service. Well, that statement is quite parliamentary; my hon. friend has a perfect right to that opinion if he chooses to express it, but it is not justified by the facts. I think the ordinary, average, intelligent civil servant, and they are an intelligent body, realizes the situation as well as the government itself does. While he has to suffer because of this cut, as some of the rest of us do, he is prepared to meet the necessities of the case.
While there is much more I should like to say, I do not want to impede the progress of a measure for which I happen at the moment to be responsible. Let me impress upon the house the fact that I entertain most profoundly the hope that we shall never again be called upon to meet an emergent situation by an emergent measure of this kind. For the sake not only of the government of the day but of the country as well, and the welfare of the civil service, I hope we shall not be called upon again to deal with a measure such as this. When we are in committee of the whole I think I shall be able to demonstrate to the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Yeniot) and one or two others who made observations to-day that this restoration means something more than they think it does. It affects eighteen thousand people, and it matters not whether they be called civil servants or what their designation or classification may be, they are employees of the government. They are now being placed in precisely the same position as they were before any salary deduction took place. Whatever complaints may have been made as to the manner in which this deduction applied in the first instance, I do not think any legitimate complaint can be made as to the circumstance that, when the time came that we could consider a restoration, small though it may be, we have first taken care of those in the humbler ranks. And we will reach those in the higher ranks, who are best able to stand it, as soon as opportunity reasonably permits.
Motion agreed to and bill read the second time.
