subtopic: THE DISCOUNT AND LOAN CORPORATION OP CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before the house asks hon. members to sanction certain privileges to some money lending interests, which privileges I do not think are in the interests of Canada. Similar bills have come before the house on other occasions, and unfortunately some have passed. Last year a bill very similar to the present one was placed before the banking and commerce committee, and was there subjected to considerable criticism; afterwards in the house the bill was thoroughly discussed and eventually defeated. I do not know how this bill has reached this stage, but inasmuch as it is now before the house for third reading I am afforded an opportunity of saying something with regard to this type of legislation.
In my opinion the bill should have gone to the banking and commerce committee. How it passed through committee of the whole I do not know. If it had gone to the banking and commerce committee I am quite sure an amendment would have been suggested and possibly passed at that stage. Looking through the bill I find it is very similar to two bills which came before the banking and commerce committee only yesterday. Apparently the whole idea behind the legislation is to enable certain money lending interests to lend financial assistance to those whom we may describe as down and out, and who cannot get any help or support from the ordinary banking institutions. In subparagraph (i) of section 3 I find provision for a rate of interest of no more than seven per cent. At first sight this looks very harmless indeed, because under our banking laws the same rate is allowed. But upon further investigation I find that two per cent is allowed for expenses. Subparagraph (ii) provides:
Charge and deduct, in addition to interest as aforesaid, for expenses to be incurred by the company for administration, including overhead, keeping of records, professional advice, correspondence and other like matters, two per centum of the principal amount of the loan.
It seems to me that the banking institutions of Canada have exactly that same work to do before making a loan, and if they charge more than seven per cent we penalize them.
In the present instance, however, it is suggested that the corporation in question should be allowed to charge another two per cent in addition to the seven per cent, because of the work falling to their lot. In the new Bank Act, supported by the government of the day, we have seen fit under section 91 to provide severe penalties if the banks charge more than the rate of seven per cent. Yet this bill asks parliament not only to permit the charging of seven per cent, but to permit an additional charge of two per cent to do the work done by the bank under the original seven per cent.
That is not all. In subparagraph (iii) I find provision for a fee not exceeding $10 for sundry services. Furthermore, interest is deducted from the principal before the principal is given to the borrower. This in itself means that the borrower is penalized for a good deal more than the rate called for in the bill. He does not get the full principal, but gets a sum less interest and other charges.
Further, if the unfortunate borrower happens to be so lucky as to be able to repay the loan before the due date he can do so only on condition that the lender has the option of deducting three months' interest. These various interests added together total about thirty-eight per cent. When we put stringent regulations and penalties in our Bank Act to prohibit banking institutions charging more than seven per cent surely parliament is not going to allow a loan corporation to lend money to probably the poorest of our people at a rate of about thirty-eight per cent interest. I have known of people in western Canada who borrowed at the rate of eight per cent or nine per cent compound interest. Once those people got into the hands of the moneylenders they found it most difficult to get out. Therefore I oppose any bill such as the present one which is likely to force borrowers to pay such high rates. I oppose it because I believe that only in very few cases will the borrower ever get out of the clutches of the moneylender. I therefore move:
That the bill be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole with instructions that they have power to amend it as follows:	Insert the
following paragraph immediately after subparagraph (iii) at page 3 of the bill, namely, IV "In no case shall the total charges for interest and additional charges exceed thirteen per cent per annum."

It has often been in my mind to dissent from a view frequently expressed in this house, but hitherto I have refrained. That view is based seemingly on the belief that all industry exists for the purpose of paying wages-that we run our railways to pay wages; that we carry on our industry to pay wages, and that our farms are operated to pay wages. I wish to dissent most emphatically from that view. This afternoon the contrary view was expressed by the hon. members for Comox-Alberni and Moose Jaw. Wages or salaries are simply one of the factors which enter into the expense of carrying on industry, whether it be private industry or
[Mr. Rhodes 1
government business. The idea that industry can be brought back to a prosperous condition by paying high wages is, to my mind, beginning at the wrong end. It is putting the cart before the horse. I should be only too happy if Canada were in a position to pay high wages. But let us consider the position on the farm. I know perfectly well that we cannot bring farming back to a prosperous condition by beginning to pay higher wages. Unfortunately, and much against our will on the farm we have had to reduce wages. The most prosperous time on the farm was the time when we were paying high wages; those wages were demanded of us when times were good. Certainly we would be glad to go back to those days. What applies to the farm I believe applies with equal force to other industries and to matters of government. I agree with the statement made this afternoon by the Minister of Finance, namely that to pay high wages to one class in the community, thereby increasing its purchasing power, we must take it out of another class by taxation. I know that idea is combated by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River and other hon. members at the end of the chamber. My firm conviction, however, is that just as farming cannot be made prosperous by beginning to pay high wages, neither can any other industry.
This afternoon when we were discussing the motion for second reading I called attention to the fact that I thought one section of the public service was being unduly discriminated against in the matter of salary deduction. My point was taken up by the former Postmaster General, a man thoroughly familiar with the whole situation. He stated the case very much better than I could have hoped to do, because in these matters I have not the knowledge possessed by the former minister. Let me, however, state the facts about one case which has come to my attention-I am not going to say it is an accurate statement of facts, but I give them as they are given to me. Certainly under such circumstances it would seem that revenue postmasters are being treated with some unfairness. For instance the person whose case I now put before the committee has stated that the postmaster's gross salary is $2,000 and that after a ten per cent deduction amounting to $200 the net amount received is $1,800. From that amount this man has to pay an assistant's salary of $500, fuel expenses $150, lighting $60, caretaking and insurance $100, reducing the net income to $990. If that is anything like a correct statement of the facts it will be perfectly plain to all hon. members that a ten per cent deduction from the gross

Civil Service-Salary Deduction
receipts of this man has the result of subjecting him to a much higher deduction than that taken from any other class of public employees.
I am glad that in this measure the government has introduced the principle of setting a minimum from which there shall be no deduction. It will be remembered that when action was taken by the government two years ago to reduce the salaries, the contention was strongly urged that that system should be adopted. To some extent that principle is now recognized. So that, for my part, while I do not like to lose that extra $400 which hon. members would like to have received all these years, I cannot protest against the general purpose the government has had in view in adopting this legislation, much as we may dislike the effect it has had upon our indemnities.

subtopic: SALARY DEDUCTION ACT-RESTORATION OF TEN PER CENT CUT TO EMPLOYEES RECEIVING $1,000 OR LESS
speechtext:
I am afraid I cannot
agree with the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Brown), that civil servants may be receiving either more than or as much as they are entitled to receive. I believe that in the civil servants of Canada we have a body of men and women who are entitled to anything that we can afford to pay them, within reason. I recognize the necessity of the government's attempting to balance the budget. But based on the very optimistic remarks made by the Minister of Finance upon the presentation of his budget, and particularly upon certain remarks made by the Minister of Railways and the Minister of Trade and Commerce before the electors of South Oxford, we are naturally entitled to come to the conclusion that conditions in Canada are on the up grade. I am one who believes that we are on the up grade. I believe also that the main responsibility for giving added impetus to the present trend rests with the government. The government have recognized this to some extent in the clause exempting from the cut the salaries of $1,000 and under. I think they should have gone much further. My own view is that they should have returned the whole ten per cent deduction. That would have done much to give encouragement to every class of the community throughout the country. I believe also that it is in the interests of the Canadian people that the government should return as soon as possible-it should have been done before now-the statutory increases which they have withheld and are withholding from the civil service. The government should also return to the system of giving the civil service the promotions which they have earned.
The main basis of my remarks, Mr. Chairman, is not that the civil service is overpaid or underpaid. I think the government have the responsibility to go as far as they possibly can in encouraging industry throughout Canada to-day and in encouraging people all over this dominion to spend the money they are withholding from the market.
With reference to the high wages referred to by my hon. friend who has just preceded me, I would point out to him that it is not a question of high wages or low wages; it is a question of relative purchasing power. We all recognize that the farmers of Canada today have a low purchasing power. We also recognize that the farmers of Canada to-day, particularly the wheat growers of the west, have received government aid on many occasions. I can speak perhaps for some of the industries that have not received a five cent bonus on wheat and other assistance. The lumber industry has not received the encouragement that even the grain growing industry has received in Canada, and yet the lumbering industry is quite prepared to shoulder its full share, I am sure, if the government will give that encouragement to industry which it should in the present circumstances.
I am again going to suggest to the minister that in my opinion there is a grave responsibility on the part of the government at this particular time to give added impetus to industry by seriously considering returning to the civil service of Canada the deduction which is being continued by this bill.

speechtext:
Last session
when the salary deduction measure was before the house I made a plea for the lower grade civil servants. I am thankful that the government in their wisdom have seen fit to restore the deduction to civil servants receiving salaries less than $1,000. It might have been better if the minimum had been placed a little higher, but the decision must be left to hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches, who are in a better position than the ordinary member to know the actual financial condition of the country.
I was glad to hear the explanation that was given by the Minister of Finance with regard to sessional labour. Another class which should be given the same consideration is the labourers, teamsters and such who are working, for example, at the experimental farms. From the interpretation given tonight by the minister I should judge that they are to be given the same treatment.
I realize quite well that in the constituency which I have the honour to represent there are mechanics and labourers who have had a much larger reduction in their income than ten per cent. In fact, many of them are still out of work. The farmers in my constituency and the dairymen who live closer to Ottawa are selling milk from their farms to the distributor for something like 76 cents per hundred pounds, which is two cents for milk that is being delivered to the consumer at ten cents a quart. I have no doubt, however, that they will be looked after by another committee of this house that is now sitting.
[Mr. Hanbury.l
I have sympathy with the civil servant who is receiving a little more than the $1,000 and does not share in the restoration of salary provided for the lower paid employees. I have sympathy also for others who are working in this city, the street railway men, for example, who received a reduction of ten per cent in their wages which up to the present has not been restored, and whose working conditions were changed so that one man now runs an electric car which two men ran some years ago. That means a further reduction for them. In addition they have to take one day off every two weeks, which means a still further reduction. I have sympathy with these people as well as with the civil service, and I wonder if there are not other members who feel the same way. I know the sympathy that some members have for the civil service, and how they plead for them at a time like this almost with tears in their eyes, but do not mind getting a summons out for a man who drives his neighbour to work in his automobile instead of letting him pay street car fare.
I wish to congratulate the government on making a move in the right direction. I firmly and honestly believe, after the statement made by the Minister of Finance tonight, that when this time comes around next year the salary cut will be completely restored and everybody will be happy. I hope that that will apply to other concerns in this city at the same time.

subtopic: SALARY DEDUCTION ACT-RESTORATION OF TEN PER CENT CUT TO EMPLOYEES RECEIVING $1,000 OR LESS
speechtext:
We are delighted to have a comparison made between conditions in private enterprise in the city of Ottawa and in the civil service, but I do not see, Mr. Chairman, what it has to do with this bill. If my hon. friend from Carleton has any grievance against any member of this house or against any private individual in Ottawa I suggest that he go down Sparks street at nine o'clock to-morrow morning and get a crowd around him and fight it out there. This is not the place. We are not interested.
My views with regard to the civil service salary deduction are very well known. Unlike the hon. member for Carleton I have always opposed this ten per cent deduction. Although I live a thousand miles away from Ottawa and from my hon. friend's constituents, a number of whom I believe, are civil servants, I have always been against this deduction of ten per cent. I believed from the first that it was not in the best interests of the country to make this deduction. But of course I understand my hon. friend's position;

Civil Service-Salary Deduction
as a supporter of the government he must get up and try to express views in line with what his government and his party think.
I do not think for one moment that the country has gained at all by making this ten per cent deduction. I said two years ago, and again last year, that the very fact that the government was the first employer in this country to reduce wages by ten per cent would mean, and it has meant, that tens of millions of dollars would be taken out of the pockets of the workmen of this country. The result is that the -whole country suffers.
The Minister of Railways asked the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard whether it was not a fact that the wages of the lumbermen had been reduced in the last two or three years. The minister seems to forget that there is quite a difference between the wages paid by private concerns and those paid by the government. Let me say to the minister that every civil servant in this country has a contract with the government. The ordinary' lumberman in the bush or the man employed by a private concern has no contract, but every civil servant has a contract when he accepts a position. Advertisements are issued, applications are asked for, claims are considered by the civil service commission or the government, and when a decision is arrived at, the man or woman has a contract. He or she has a contract just the same as I have. The people of this country promised to pay me S4,000 per year to represent them in this parliament. I have always contended that I am entitled to that $4,000 and that this government had no right to reduce my sessional indemnity' to $3,600.
Mr. McINTO-SH: Sue the government.

subtopic: SALARY DEDUCTION ACT-RESTORATION OF TEN PER CENT CUT TO EMPLOYEES RECEIVING $1,000 OR LESS
speechtext:
They would not issue a fiat. Let me tell the minister that the civil servant is in an entirely different position from that of the man in the bush or the man working in a private enterprise. Civil servants, whether they be stenographers, elevator men, charwomen, lighthouse keepers or anything else, have a solemn contract with the government. The Prime Minister often speaks of the sanctity of contracts. I say to the Minister of Railways: Go and consult the Prime Minister and ask him where is the sanctity of contracts in this bill or in those of the last two years. Subsection (b) of section 2 defines a member of the public service as follows:
"Member of the public service of Canada" means every officer, clerk and employee in any branch or portion of the public service of Canada, to whom any compensation is paid, *either directly or indirectly, out of the revenue
of His Majesty in respect of his government of Canada, other than the Governor General of Canada, the lieutenant governors of the several provinces of Canada, the members of the judiciary, and the members of the military, naval and air forces of Canada, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and includes members of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada.
I should like to know if it is intended that the governor general, the lieutenant governors, the members of the judiciary and the members of the military', naval and air forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are to receive their full salaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SALARY DEDUCTION ACT-RESTORATION OF TEN PER CENT CUT TO EMPLOYEES RECEIVING $1,000 OR LESS
speechtext:
I am sure we must all pay tribute to the consistency of the hon. member for Antigonsh-Guysborough throughout the years that we have had to consider such bills as the one now under consideration. He has left no doubt as to his attitude with respect to this and the measures of previous years. Whether or not we agree with him, we must give him credit for making his position so clear. It may be that when one enters the public service he has a contract, but I do not feel myself in a position to argue as to the legal position of that contract. I think the overriding question of the public need is the consideration which has governed. The people of the mother country have as keen an appreciation of the sanctity of contracts as any people on earth, and yet under precisely the same conditions, Great Britain reduced the salaries of some of her higher paid members of the judiciary by as much as twenty per cent, of her cabinet ministers by a like amount, of her school teachers by fifteen per cent and of the members in the other services by substantial percentages. Whether or not hon. gentlemen are in agreement with us, we have assumed it to be in the public interest to make this deduction in order to meet an emergent situation.
With respect to the specific question asked by my hon. friend, I may say that ever since the first salary deduction act the Governor General has voluntarily sent his cheque regularly for ten per cent of the full amount of his salary. The members of the judiciary and of the naval and, military forces are not touched by this bill, but there is another bill touching their salaries which will bring about a similar result. This bill makes a straight salary deduction, but a companion bill which will follow contains a provision for a special income tax to amount to ten per cent of the salaries of these individuals. It will be in terms similar to the bill of last year, and it will cover all those in the list except the

Civil Service-Salary Deduction
lieutenant governors. For reasons which I need not at this moment discuss at length, it was felt that as representatives of His Majesty they should not be placed in the same position as those who had been cut.

subtopic: SALARY DEDUCTION ACT-RESTORATION OF TEN PER CENT CUT TO EMPLOYEES RECEIVING $1,000 OR LESS
speechtext: I have a matter which I should like to bring to the attention of the government. This may not be the proper time to do it and, if not, I should be glad to be informed as to when would be the proper time. In some parts of the country there are government institutions such as experimental farms. Those employed on these farms are paid by the dominion government. In some cases they live in houses which are the property of the government and that property does not pay any tax. This imposes a very heavy burden upon the school systems. The matter was brought to my attention a month or so ago when it was pointed out that a large number of employees of the government in a certain place were living on government property. In that same place a large number of children were attending the public school, imposing a heavy burden upon the people of that community, many of them very poor, yet having to pay taxes out of their very small incomes to support the schools at which the children of government employees were receiving education, without cost to themselves or the government. If it is at all possible I suggest that in all such cases the government should see that a school tax in some form be paid so as to ease the burden of taxpayers in such communities. That is the situation that prevails in some of the provinces, although I am told to-night that there are some provinces in which an arrangement is made for the payment of some special tax. I suggest that in all cases where employees of the government live on property on which no taxes are paid and enjoy the benefit of schools the government should impose an obligation on those receiving remuneration to contribute to the school tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SALARY DEDUCTION ACT-RESTORATION OF TEN PER CENT CUT TO EMPLOYEES RECEIVING $1,000 OR LESS
speechtext:
I do not take exception in the main to the attitude of my hon. friend, but I must point out to him that he raises at once the larger question as to how far crown property ought to be exempt from taxation. I do not suppose it would do much good to enter into a discussion of that phase of the matter; that is a recognized principle and we need not go into the reasons for it. But where there are employees living on crown property under such conditions as the hon. member has depicted, the right to live in those houses forms a portion of the compensation, and the amount of cash which the 
employee receives is diminished to the extent of the allowance made for his so living. In the main that compensation is fixed by the civil service commission for various classes of the public service living on government property throughout the country.

speechtext: As my hon. friend rightly says, there is no good reason why such a person whose children enjoy the privileges of the public school should not be called upon to pay his share of the school rates the same as other people living in the community. Whether there is any governmental action which can be taken or is required in the circumstances, I am not in a position at the moment to say, because so far as I am concerned the matter has never been raised before. But from the point of view of the community, in equity and in simple justice such an employee ought to pay his fair share of the school rates.

subtopic: SALARY DEDUCTION ACT-RESTORATION OF TEN PER CENT CUT TO EMPLOYEES RECEIVING $1,000 OR LESS
speechtext:
I accept very gladly the explanation which the Minister of Finance has made with reference to the various staffs of the house. The information which I received may have been right at the time, but a different construction has been placed upon it, and I congratulate the minister on this extension of generosity. I never took the words of the hon. gentleman to mean any lecture to me this afternoon; he would have had to speak in a very much different tone to lead me to believe that he was trying to lecture me. I like his cold steel; he is a gallant foe; I have had many a tiff with him, but I have managed to come out without being either too much scared or too much scarred.
The hon. member for Lisgar has stated the situation from his point of view, but I would say to him and particularly to the hon. member for Moose Jaw-and this applies to a slight degree to the Minister of Finance: O consistency, what crimes have been committed in thy name! It happens that in the constituency of Lisgar there are a certain number of rural postmasters and therefore there is a duty incumbent, and properly so, on the distinguished member for Lisgar, to look after their particular interests. It happens that in the city of Ottawa there is but one postmaster, but there are hundreds of letter carriers. Well, why should not what is good for the rural postmasters be also good for the city letter carriers? It happens that in Ottawa there are twenty or twenty-five per cent of the classified civil servants of the dominion.

Civil Sertrice-Salary Deduction
If instead of having that percentage of civil servants in Ottawa we had so many farmers or brickmakers or textile workers or manufacturers, then I doubt very much that as many hon. members of this house who are prone to hit upon, this city and upon the civil servants would take the same attitude. Why not be consistent, therefore? This city has a population of 136,000 and of that number there may be 10,000 employed in some line of industry, be it match making or soap making or forging or in the civil service or as grocers, and if these particular interests are not in conflict with the general interest, then surely there is a duty incumbent on those whose honour and privilege it is to represent these people in this house to see that their particular interests are properly safeguarded, provided that the general interest of others is not jeopardized. That is the stand I have consistently taken.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw said that the city of Ottawa does not know anything about depression. Well, I am not here to say unpleasant things about the city of Ottawa or of any other city. I am not here to expose the evils or those charitable cases that are being looked after. This is not the time and place, and it is not my particular duty to do so in this house. But I would point out that in Ottawa there has been a tremendous amount of direct relief expended through the government, by private parties, by social and religious organizations!, and voluntarily by the civil servants to a considerable proportion of their salaries, though they have been cut ten per cent. True, it is not quite as apparent around Ottawa that there is as much depression or as much hardship as one might see elsewhere, but let me say that though the wound may be concealed it does not mean that it is not as painful as one that is exposed, and very often there is much more bitterness added in trying to conceal it than to show it.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw also said that so long as the western people suffered, he did not want the cut to be restored. Well, I have more consideration for the western farmer and more sympathy for the business people of the rest of the dominion than some members have for a certain portion of the community. I deplore their misery; I deplore the misery of the farmer, of the industrial wage earner, but I ask: How much has the $8,700,000 that was taken away from the civil servants helped those poor people, and also how much has the $2,500,000 from Ottawa helped to alleviate their suffering? I am sure it must have mitigated it to a certain extent
if one considers how some hon. members desire that the cut be not returned. I think I have some reason to say for the city of Ottawa: Hands off the civil service.
The Minister of Finance this afternoon said that if we transfer the $8,700,000 from the pockets of the taxpayer, that is simply a matter of bookkeeping. I pointed out before in that connection that the government was able to collect $8,000,000 or $9,000,000 by simply moving the decimal point in the books and that it did not cost one-hundredth of one per cent to collect that amount. There never before has been any collection agency, any bond selling or issuing of a loan for the government that has cost it so little. It is quite proper for hon. members to take this attitude if they think it is going to benefit themselves, but let me put the matter in this way: If the civil service not only of Ottawa but of Canada as a whole is to be taxed in that manner to the extent of ten per cent and if that sum of $8,700,000 is applied on the public debt or to help to balance the budget, then why in the name of goodness and of justice did the large industrial corporations when they made the deductions they did from the wages of their employees, not take that money to the Minister of Finance and say: Here is our fair share; just as the civil service have paid their portion into your hands, so we pay ours that you may be helped in solving your financial difficulties, in balancing the budget and in alleviating the suffering that exists? But they did not do that, and the minister knows well that none of all the wage deductions that have been made by private enterprise has found its way into the coffers of the state to help relieve his financial troubles. But if that course had been followed; if the money taken from those whose salaries were cut had been paid into the coffers of the state, then of course the civil servants of Canada would feel somewhat relieved in knowing that they were not the only ones that were being mulct to this extent.
The Minister of Finance said lastly that the wages and salaries of the civil servants must come out of the pockets of the taxpayer, but one would think the civil servant simply drew his salary and did no work-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SALARY DEDUCTION ACT-RESTORATION OF TEN PER CENT CUT TO EMPLOYEES RECEIVING $1,000 OR LESS

subtopic: SALARY DEDUCTION ACT-RESTORATION OF TEN PER CENT CUT TO EMPLOYEES RECEIVING $1,000 OR LESS

I know the minister does not mean that; it is absolutely inconsistent with the words of eulogy which he uttered, and quite properly, with respect to the civil service this afternoon, which he knows they deserve. That is what the minister says, but

Civil Service-Salary Deduction
others who are not in his position, and who do not understand the situation as he does, put a different construction on the matter, and it is not fair. When the civil service of Canada works, it works for the benefit of the state. Civil servants are servants of the state; they serve not only Ottawa but the whole of Canada when they earn their wages, and there ought to be a feeling of pride on the part of everyone, whether from the eastern or the western provinces, or from the north or the south, to know that while goverments come and governments go, while one ministry falls and another takes its place, the civil service of Canada carries on its work just the same. The backbone of the Canadian public service to-day is the presence in it of men of long years of experience, men who have served loyally under Grit and Tory, Liberal and Conservative administrations. Therefore these people are entitled, for the sole reason that they have served the state loyally, to be so treated any time a question concerning them is brought up.
Having said that much, I have only one question to ask the minister so that he may reply when he speaks again. He said that some 18.000 would be affected. Some days ago I placed a question on the order paper, but it was turned, and quite properly, into a return. I do not know that I shall get the answer in time, and I should like to ask whether the minister can inform me as to the units that go to make the total. I should like to know how the 18.000 are made up, and what amount will be paid to each.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SALARY DEDUCTION ACT-RESTORATION OF TEN PER CENT CUT TO EMPLOYEES RECEIVING $1,000 OR LESS
speechtext:
May I at once say to the senior member for Ottawa that I do not take exception to his attitude on this question; on the contrary I commend him for championing as a representative of Ottawa the cause of a large number of those who are his constituents. He is doing only the right and proper thing as a representative who has in mind the interests of those who sent him to parliament. But I do object very seriously to his placing in my mouth words which I never uttered, and drawing therefrom inferences which cannot properly be drawn from the words which I did use. When I said that the civil servants are paid out of the pockets of the taxpayers of Canada I did not for one moment raise the question of the propriety of that being so; on the contrary,
I am the first to concede to my hon. friend that I know many, many in the civil service who, even if they had their full salary restored, would still be earning more than they

were receiving. There are many in the service who are underpaid even at their full salary. At the same time there are some civil servants who would be overpaid if they got S100 a year; they are, however, in the great minority. For the civil service at large I have nothing but the greatest admiration, and I admit at once that by and large they earn their salaries. If my hon. friend were fair- I am not suggesting for a moment he intended to be unfair, but he was-he would have acknowledged that I did not use the argument in the connection he suggested. The hon. member for Kindersley had said that if we restored the salaries it would have increased the purchasing power of the civil servants by $7.8!X).COO a year. What I said was that the civil servants were paid out of the pockets of the taxpayers and that all the restoration of salary would do, so far as purchasing power was concerned, would be to transfer it from the taxpayer, whose purchasing power would be that much less, to the civil servant, whose purchasing power would be that much more, and that at the end we would be no further ahead than when we started. That was what I had in mind when I made the remark that the civil servants were paid out of the pockets of the taxpayers.
With respect to my hon. friend's direct question, the officials of the department tell me that to make an exact allocation of the number affected in the city of Ottawa would take a very long time, because it means the conning of some sixty thousand names. The best estimate I can secure from those most versed in civil service affairs in Ottawa is that it wall affect somewhere between fifteen hundred and two thousand individuals in Ottawm.

the chances are that the greater number would be in the class above $1,000, my hon. friend, whose knowledge of the civil service is probably more intimate than that of most persons outside of. the civil service itself, will be able perhaps to make some rough deduction until such time as we can get a more accurate figure.
Mr. MaeINNIS:	I wish to thank the
minister for the assurance he gave a few minutes ago that those civil servants who are not getting over $1,000 a year, regardless of whether or not they are full time employees, will not be subject to the deduction. That will be a welcome assurance to many civil servants.
The hon. member for Lisgar said that the purpose of industry is not the payment of wages. But he stopped there and did not tell us what the purpose of industry is, so we are no wiser than before. In my opinion the purpose of industry is to produce the things that the community needs, and the things so produced are distributed in part through the payment of wages. I know very well that the owners of industry regret every cent they have to pay in wages, but I also know, whether they do or not, that if they did not pay any wages at all their condition would be much worse even than it is now. There is no possible way of keeping industry going unless we provide the means of distributing the product. It is being distributed to-day largely through salaries and wages. What has happened is that our ability to produce has increased and is increasing every day, and as it increases we are reducing our ability to distribute the product. Because of that the economic condition of the people becomes more and more the concern of government. We have noticed that in the last few years, in the extent to which the government has had to take steps to relieve the effects of the inability of industry to distribute its own product. If wages were reduced still more the position of the farmer would be worse, because he would be still less able to sell what he produces. Therefore I say it is of real concern to the government to see that the means of distribution of goods and services produced in the country are maintained. For that reason the government should make provision that those in its own service shall be adequately recompensed, so as to help relieve the depression in industry. We find that in the United States the depression was raised only when they took steps to raise wages. In Great Britain they had to do the same thing,
and I am quite satisfied that we in this country will have also to do it.
Hon. members talk about the poor taxpayer. The fact is that taxation will have to be used as a means of further equalizing the present inequitable distribution of goods. It is being so used in Great Britain, where the greater portion of the larger incomes is taken in order to distribute better the products of industry. The hon. member for Lisgar will have to revise his economics before he finds a solution of the problem confronting the people to-day, the problem of misery and want in the midst of the greatest abundance that the world has ever seen.

I was particularly pleased this afternoon to hear the Minister of Finance say that he was a believer in high wages and high prices and that the countries in which high wages and high prices exist were the countries which gave the most comforts to ordinary citizens. I heartily concur in that statement. I was pleased also to hear that ten per cent was not to be taken off those receiving less than 31,000. My own view and wish of course would have been to see the ten per cent restored on salaries under 32,000. However, the minister has pointed out that in his opinion and in the opinion of the government conditions do not warrant such a change. While I am and always have been an advocate of high wages, and have persistently fought for high wages throughout my life, I believe this would be the proper time to view the great spread between the salaries received by a certain class of civil servants and other classes. We have a class of civil servants in this dominion under the heading of deputy ministers to whom we are paying in salaries a total of 3275,000 a year, and I never hear anyone in this house protesting against the great spread between the $9,000 a year received by some of these deputy ministers and the $3,500 a year received by other civil servants who are just as capable. There are thirty men rated here at cost of over 3275,000 a year, and in addition the country is contributing a certain amount of their superannuation. Very many of these men will be retired on a higher superannuation allowance than most men can earn in a whole year. Some of them receive an annual superannuation allowance of 36,000. I say that without fear of contradiction. If there was any possibility of the lower grade civil servants ever working up to a salary of $9,000, I for one would never raise my voice in protest, but when one considers that these $9,000 positions are just political appointments calling for men of no greater calibre than many heads of branches who are receiving only $3,600, although just as capable, I cannot help but express my feeling that it is time we reviewed this salary question very carefully. If we are ever going to put our house in order now is the time to do it. Let me repeat, in order that I shall not be misunderstood, that I am not against paying high wages or paying what a man is worth, but there is too wide a gap between a certain class of civil servants occupying high positions and that other large group which unless something is done can never be jumped and never will be, because in the majority of cases the higher offices to which I refer are just straight political appointments.

There is another point. I understand that an order in council was passed some time ago by the government that civil servants of the age of sixty-five years or over should be discharged or superannuated. If I am wrong I hope the minister will correct me. Some time ago I put a question on the order paper regarding this order in council, and a return was brought down to the house which makes interesting reading. What makes me rise on this occasion is what I consider an injustice in connection with an order of this kind. I am not at this time entering into the merits or demerits of the question whether a man of sixty-five or over should or should not be dismissed, but I do take the ground that once an order of that kind has been made there should be no favorites played. Many men who are sixty-five and over have retained their positions due to a certain amount of pull, while others who have not that pull have been dismissed and I feel that it is my duty to protest. I may be wrong in my impression about the order in council to which I refer. The return tabled in the house on April 9 shows the total number of civil servants discharged and superannuated under that order in council applying to employees sixty-five years and over. This was my question:
1.	What was the total number of civil servants and' government employees discharged and superannuated under the ruling regarding all employees 65 years and over?
2.	What were the numbers discharged and superannuated respectively, in each department of the public service since the order came into effect?
3.	How many persons 65 years of age or over, are still in the employ of the government?
4.	What are the names of the said persons, and in what respective departments of the public service are they engaged?
The return that was brought down in reply gives a table showing in the first column the number superannuated or retired, in the second column the number discharged, and in the third column the number still engaged. I find that 506 w-ere superannuated or retired and 58 discharged, and that 1,020 are still engaged. In looking over the names I find that men have been retained who do not occupy a key position. My complaint is not that they are retained, but that the order in council is not applied impartially, that one man with a little pull is retained and a man without pull let go. I could cite instances of men who have been retained in the public service because of a little influence they had, while immigration inspectors, customs and excise officers, clerks, cooks, charwomen, blacksmiths, and so forth right through the list

have been let go. I know captains of dredges who have been let out in my district because they have reached the age of sixty-five, while I find others have been retained. I would like the minister to explain why this order in council has been carried out in the way it has.

My hon. friend from New Westminster is probably aware of the fact that it has been the law for many years that it is competent upon the recommendation of a minister of the crown for the government to retire any employee who arrives at the age of sixty-five, and no special or general order in council is required for that purpose. The order in council to which my hon. friend refers had reference only to those civil servants who were sixty-five years or over and whose services could be dispensed with, and whose places it would not be necessary to fill. It was solely from the viewpoint of economy and efficiency in the public service that that order in council was passed. In each instance the individual retired received a retiring gratuity. In fact, in the view of the auditor general, who made official complaint in the matter, the government was over generous and exceeded its power in giving a larger gratuity than he thought the law warranted.
I cannot speak for all departments of the government; I can only speak for my own. Although it is not a pleasant duty to be associated with a policy which calls for the retirement, even with a gratuity, of those who have reached the age of sixty-five, it is difficult for one administering a department, having in mind his duty to the state, to justify continuing in the public service and paying full salary to one who is doing work that can be done by others in the department without adding to their numbers and without burdening unduly those who remain in the service. I would welcome from my hon. friend the slightest evidence that so far as my department is concerned there was any kind of pull whatever in the matter. I accepted without question the advice I received from responsible officers of my department in whom I had and still have the fullest confidence. I am not suggesting for one moment that there may not be individual cases where pull may have been exercised. We are all human. We know the atmosphere which surrounds the public service and which it is difficult to eradicate, but I would venture the belief that in the main, in the great majority of cases, the retirements were made in conformity with the idea which was in mind at the time the order in council was passed.

My hon. friend has referred to the fact that a number of others have been retained in the public service who are over sixty-five years of age. Certainly. We did not desire that any man who was performing a useful public service should be retired because he was sixty-five, and that was specifically provided for. The order in council had reference only to those whose positions did not require to be filled, in other words, those who were surplus in the department. Nor did it apply to those sixty-five years of age who were occupying administrative posts which they could properly fill. I have in mind members of the public service over seventy years of age who had to be retained by special votes in the estimates, but they are men who are singularly young for their years, who have acquired wide knowledge in the service and are of singular use to the public service, and it was believed that it was in the public interest that their services should be retained. I hope I have covered the ground that I should cover in answering to the best of my ability the question of the hon. member for New Westminster.

In these circumstances the government would leave itself open to every conceivable kind of pressure and criticism if it did or did not act at a given time with respect to the restoration of the balance. This does not apply to my hon. friend, but in view of the criticism which we have received ad lib from hon. gentlemen opposite with respect to the blank cheque, and considering the objection they attach thereto, I am rather surprised at the suggestion that there should be such a power as that placed in the hands of the government.

subtopic: SALARY DEDUCTION ACT-RESTORATION OF TEN PER CENT CUT TO EMPLOYEES RECEIVING $1,000 OR LESS
speechtext: But this would be specified in the act, that in six months' time action shall be taken if the increasing revenues justify it. I do think the minister's argument rather weak when he says that the set-up of the finances is based on the assumption he states and therefore he cannot depart from it. The set-up of the finances in the last several yearn past has totally failed to come up to his estimate and nothing in particular has happened. Cheerfully and hopefully he anticipates, as he says in the budget, that the returns in the ensuing months will run higher than he has calculated either in the past or in his set-up, and I have no doubt that he will cheerfully accept the increased revenue in the months to come if it eventuates. Well, surely he can anticipate action on such increased revenue. He will not repudiate the increased revenues as they come in,, and therefore I do not see why he should not consider the suggestion. With all deference to the minister, I submit that the argument as to his being unable to depart from an arranged set-up is rather weak.

That no provision of this act shall operate to reduce the compensation of any member of the public service of Canada below $1,000 per annum.	[DOT]

speechtext: The first provision is intended to deal with the borderline cases and the second one is the general exemption. subtopic: SALARY DEDUCTION ACT-RESTORATION OF TEN PER CENT CUT TO EMPLOYEES RECEIVING $1,000 OR LESS

That is rather

Does the minister think it is advisable that such a provision dealing with civil service appropriations should be placed in the body of the bill? This house has not voted the civil list for any department. That civil list contains first of all salaries, and secondly contingencies, and it seems to me it could easily be provided that the money that may be needed should be voted by parliament instead of being paid out of the consolidated revenue fund. Inasmuch as each department will have to deal with any adjustment that may have to be made in the salary of any one of the civil servants that may be affected, why not provide in the body of the act for the money to be paid out of departmental contingencies vote? The contingencies vote authorizes the payment of travelling expenses of civil servants. Surely therefore, if you amended this bill to provide that any adjustment required would be met out of the contingencies vote, you would avoid creating the precedent, which is now being established, of dealing with the matter out of the consolidated revenue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SALARY DEDUCTION ACT-RESTORATION OF TEN PER CENT CUT TO EMPLOYEES RECEIVING $1,000 OR LESS

My hon. friend has had
a very wide experience in the public service, but I would point out to him that there is nothing unusual in this provision. He may not have found it in a salary bill of this kind, but he will find it in numerous statutes passed by parliament. Now, the reason for this is twofold. In the first place, I must direct to the attention of the committee the fact that the estimates were prepared and printed on the basis of ninety per cent, and notwithstanding what my hon. friend has said, the civil government vote has been passed in a number of instances. In the second place, the contingency vote has been reduced in most departments. But even if it were at the old figure, it could not adequately take care of the ten per cent. But there is a further reason, and it is this. A number of cases will have to be dealt with by the treasury board under the provisions particularly of subsection (c) of section 6, and money must be provided to pay the compensation in these cases. You could not, unless you put in some omnibus lump sum in a general vote, which would not get you further ahead, be able to provide by specific vote for these particular cases; whereas this means that where you can pay it out of the consolidated revenue fund there will be no excess vote but only that amount required will be taken for the compensation provided for in the restoration of salary deduction in respect of those who receive up to $1,000.

subtopic: SALARY DEDUCTION ACT-RESTORATION OF TEN PER CENT CUT TO EMPLOYEES RECEIVING $1,000 OR LESS

I quite understand the minister, but I realized during my days in the service that one of the most sacred things was the consolidated revenue fund. I can remember that it was impossible to draw any money from that fund except by governor general's warrant when the house was not in session. I realize also, as the minister says, that especially in the last three or four years there has been a tendency for us to put our hands on this special vote, called the consolidated revenue fund, and to embody in numerous acts of parliament the powers granted under this act. This deals with civil service appropriations. I think it is creating rather an awkward precedent to authorize any money to be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund for such a purpose. I believe it would be proper to provide under a special vote, either in the supplementary estimates or in the contingencies, a lump sum to be administered departmentally or by the treasury board than to place those words as they stand in the legislation. Of course I may be wrong. I can quite well understand the Minister of Finance has his own reason, but

The general estimates as submitted to the house provide for a deduction of ten per cent or for ninety per cent of the former salary. This bill completely disorganizes those estimates; it provides that up to a certain salary the amount of ten per cent as deducted in the general estimates shall be returned. The proper way to deal with the matter would be to bring in a supplementary estimate to supplement, if I may use that term, the general estimates as they now stand. In that respect the case is entirely different from that cited to the committee by the Minister of Finance. My opinion is that sufficient information could be obtained so that there could be inserted in the supplementary estimates of each department the sum necessary to cover the restoration of this ten per cent deduction. Each department ought to be able to know within a measurable distance the exact figure that would be required. I can understand that the minister is quite right in saying that certain cases will have to be readjusted in some way or another, but those cannot 
amount to such a large sum as to warrant the minister in departing from the principle of obtaining the authority of parliament in voting money for public expenditures. In view of that I have an amendment that I wish to move, seconded by the hon. member for Rimouski :
